Trust the Direction, Search the Step: Zero-and-First-Order Methods for LLM Fine-Tuning

Cristian McGee Affiliation: University of Central Florida Affiliation: Orlando, FL, USA    El Houcine Bergou Affiliation: Mohammed VI Polytechnic University Affiliation: Ben Guerir, Morocco    Aritra Dutta Affiliation: University of Central Florida Affiliation: Orlando, FL, USA
Abstract

Step-size selection remains a central challenge in large-scale neural network optimization; conservative steps slow convergence, while aggressive steps can destabilize it. We combine Zero-and-First-Order optimization (ZFO) and propose a framework that decouples direction selection from step-size. ZFO uses a trusted first-order optimizer to determine the direction and performs zeroth-order evaluations only along this one-dimensional subspace to choose how far to move. Using the current gradient information and two additional objective function evaluations, ZFO instances construct a local model of the objective function along the proposed direction and select a curvature-aware step within a bounded search interval. This yields an adaptive step-selection mechanism that costs less than a full line search. We provide theoretical guarantees to show that shared-sample evaluations produce reliable finite-difference curvature estimates, that the induced local model selects a near-optimal step along the search interval, and that ZFO converges to a neighborhood of a stationary point. Across the evaluated settings, language models and datasets, ZFO frequently improves optimization and final performance relative to fixed-step first-order baselines, with the magnitude and preferred local model depending on the objective. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/nizswan/Zeroth-First-Order-Framework.

1 Introduction

Gradient-based first-order (FO) optimization methods are the main workhorse of modern deep neural network training [14, 31, 25]. During training, gradient information provides the direction to move along, which, coupled with a step size (or learning rate), updates the model parameters. While the gradient direction is generally informative, the step size used along that direction is typically chosen through schedules, heuristics, or hyperparameter tuning [30, 18, 48, 49]. For larger networks, whose local geometry can change rapidly during adaptation, a poorly chosen step size may lead to unstable training [13]. Despite these step-size instabilities, FO methods remain the standard choice for neural network adaptation because the FO gradient provides strong directional guidance.

In contrast, zeroth-order (ZO) methods [34, 26, 38, 16, 5, 6, 17, 7] do not compute gradients. They construct approximate gradient updates using only objective function evaluations, often via finite differences along random directions. Although ZO methods reduce computational overhead, gradient approximations are often noisy and high-variance in large-dimensional settings [2, 23]. However, when FO provides the update direction, the high-dimensional problem becomes a univariate step-selection problem; see Figure 1. Consequently, computationally inexpensive ZO evaluations become substantially informative for modeling local function behavior. This raises a natural question:

If FO methods are strong at choosing an update direction, can ZO evaluations be used to decide how far to move along that direction?

We investigate this question by using ZO evaluations not to replace gradients, but to select reliable step sizes. This idea is related to recent work on generalized Newton step selection GeN [9], which uses function evaluations along a first-order direction to construct a curvature-informed step. In contrast, ZFO takes a broader view: rather than committing to a particular step construction, we formulate fixed-budget directional step selection as a local modeling problem. This perspective is not restricted to a specific optimization setup; in principle, the framework applies whenever an approximate gradient direction is available, but its appropriate magnitude is uncertain, a pattern that recurs in existing step-size rules [33]. This uncertainty becomes especially relevant in noisy or stochastic optimization settings.

Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning is a natural setting for this hybridization. Modern fine-tuning pipelines construct minibatches of prompt-response examples and optimize a surrogate objective on these fixed examples. Once a minibatch is formed, nearby parameter evaluations can reuse the same data and require only additional forward evaluations of the perturbed model. This makes ZO probes especially useful—not as a replacement for gradients, but as a cheap mechanism for modeling objective variation along a trusted FO direction. In contrast, fully ZO LLM fine-tuning methods use forward evaluations to estimate high-dimensional gradients [34, 26]. ZFO exploits this structure by assigning direction selection to a base FO optimizer, such as AdamW [31] or Muon [25], while using a small number of ZO function evaluations to build a univariate local model of the objective function and select the step size along that direction. Taken together, the ZFO framework acts as a lightweight step-selection wrapper around a standard FO optimizer. This is particularly valuable in LLM fine-tuning, where local geometry can shift rapidly and poorly tuned learning rates can cause unstable or slow training [27, 50].

Problem Setup. Let fine-tuning an LLM be represented by a conditional distribution πθ​(y∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x), where xx denotes an input prompt, yy denotes a model response, and θ∈ℝd\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are the model parameters. We initialize the model from a pretrained reference model and further optimize it using task-specific feedback. We summarize the main notation used throughout the paper in §D; see Table D.

At a given iteration tt, a FO fine-tuning algorithm constructs a minibatch of information, denoted by StS_{t}. This minibatch contains all quantities needed to define the current training objective. Depending on the method, StS_{t} may include prompts, sampled responses, supervised labels, etc. Conditioned on StS_{t}, the fine-tuning method defines a sampled surrogate objective optimized during the current update Ft​(θ)=F⁡(θ,St).F_{t}(\theta)=F(\theta;S_{t}). Different LLM fine-tuning algorithms instantiate this surrogate differently. Our framework does not require a particular choice of FtF_{t}, and only assumes that the surrogate can be evaluated on the fixed minibatch StS_{t}.

This fixed-batch viewpoint is standard in LLM fine-tuning [34, 46, 26, 22]. Once StS_{t} is constructed, it is held fixed within the update. Evaluating FtF_{t} at a nearby parameter value therefore does not require constructing a new batch or collecting new feedback; it only requires re-scoring the same prompt-response pairs under the perturbed model.

A standard fine-tuning step computes a stochastic gradient of the sampled surrogate at the current parameters, and passes it through an optimizer such as AdamW. If we denote the resulting update direction by gtg_{t}, the usual first-order gradient ascent update is: θt+1=θt+α​gt,\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}+\alpha g_{t}, where α>0\alpha>0 is the learning rate. This update contains two decisions: the direction gtg_{t} and the step length controlled by α\alpha. The chosen fine-tuning surrogate and the optimizer determine the direction. The step length, however, is usually specified by a learning-rate schedule or hyperparameter tuning [32]. In LLM fine-tuning, this scalar choice can be sensitive; overly tiny steps may not entirely use the information in the current batch, while aggressive steps can destabilize training [51].

We improve the step-length decision while leaving the optimizer direction unchanged and formulate all objectives as maximization problems. Let gt≠0g_{t}\neq 0, and define the normalized direction

zt=gt‖gt‖.z_{t}=\frac{g_{t}}{\|g_{t}\|}. (1)

We restrict the current surrogate to the one-dimensional path along this direction:

ϕt​(s)=Ft​(θt+s​zt),for​s∈ℝ.\phi_{t}(s)=F_{t}(\theta_{t}+sz_{t}),\quad{\rm for\;}s\in\mathbb{R}.

The standard optimizer step corresponds to sFO=α​‖gt‖.s_{\mathrm{FO}}=\alpha\|g_{t}\|. Thus, choosing the learning rate is equivalent to choosing a scalar displacement along the fixed-batch improvement of ϕt\phi_{t}.

Rather than relying only on a global learning-rate schedule, we ask whether the current surrogate FtF_{t} supports a better step along the direction already selected by the optimizer. We search over a bounded interval ℐt=[0,Rt],Rt=β​α​‖gt‖,\mathcal{I}_{t}=[0,R_{t}],\quad R_{t}=\beta\alpha\|g_{t}\|, where β>0\beta>0 controls the search radius relative to the baseline optimizer step. When β=1\beta=1, the interval ends at the usual first-order update; larger values allow the method to consider longer steps while remaining constrained to the same direction:

st⋆≈arg⁡maxs∈ℐt​ϕt​(s).s_{t}^{\star}\approx\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}\phi_{t}(s). (2)

A full line search would evaluate ϕt\phi_{t} at many candidate values of ss, which is costly for LLMs. Instead, we use a fixed-budget step-selection procedure: the current value ϕt​(0)\phi_{t}(0) is obtained from the usual forward evaluation of the surrogate on StS_{t}, and the backward pass gives the directional derivative ϕt′​(0)=⟨∇Ft​(θt),zt⟩.\phi_{t}^{\prime}(0)=\left\langle\nabla F_{t}(\theta_{t}),z_{t}\right\rangle. We then evaluate the same fixed-batch surrogate at two symmetric perturbations along the update direction:

ϕt​(ϵ)=Ft​(θt+ϵ​zt),ϕt​(−ϵ)=Ft​(θt−ϵ​zt), for a small ​ϵ>0.\phi_{t}(\epsilon)=F_{t}(\theta_{t}+\epsilon z_{t}),\quad\phi_{t}(-\epsilon)=F_{t}(\theta_{t}-\epsilon z_{t}),\text{ for a small }\epsilon>0.

Together, these quantities {ϕt​(0),ϕt′​(0),ϕt​(ϵ),ϕt​(−ϵ)},\left\{\phi_{t}(0),\phi_{t}^{\prime}(0),\phi_{t}(\epsilon),\phi_{t}(-\epsilon)\right\}, define a local model of the surrogate improvement along the optimizer direction. The selected step sts_{t} is obtained by maximizing this model over ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}, and the parameters are updated as θt+1=θt+st​zt.\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}+s_{t}z_{t}. In this formulation, the base LLM fine-tuning algorithm determines the surrogate FtF_{t} and the update direction gtg_{t}, while our method determines how far to move along that direction; see Figure 1. The procedure is therefore compatible with a broad class of LLM fine-tuning objectives. Due to space limitations, we defer the related work to §A.

Our contributions. We develop ZFO as a general framework that separates first-order direction selection from low-query zeroth-order step selection. This formulation allows different local step-selection models to be developed and analyzed within the same optimization framework. Below, we summarize our main contributions:

(i) A ZFO optimization framework. We propose the general ZFO framework in which a standard first-order optimizer proposes an update direction, and a small number of zeroth-order evaluations are used to choose an improved step size along this direction. Within this framework, we develop four practical ZFO instances based on Taylor and Padé local models. While existing methods such as GeN is a one step-selection rule, our ZFO is a fixed-budget directional modeling framework. GeN can be interpreted within the ZFO framework as a particular fixed-budget directional step-selection.

(ii) Theoretical justification of adaptive step selection. Our theoretical analysis of the one-dimensional objective follows from restricting the training objective to the first-order search direction. We show that the finite-difference curvature estimates with common random numbers (CRNs) concentrate around their population counterparts with high probability. We further prove that maximizing the resulting local model yields a step whose objective value is near-optimal within a bounded search region. Finally, we establish a global stationarity guarantee showing that ZFO converges to a stationary neighborhood whose size is controlled by the accumulated step-selection error.

(iii) Empirical validation across scales. We evaluate ZFO on both controlled low-dimensional problems and LLM fine-tuning tasks. The experiments show that ZFO is robust to the choice of initial learning rate and can match or outperform standard first-order and zeroth-order baselines on most benchmarks. These results demonstrate that lightweight zeroth-order step adaptation can improve the stability and reliability of first-order fine-tuning without incurring the cost of full line search or extensive hyperparameter tuning.

2 Methodology

We fix an iteration tt and suppress the subscript tt for readability. We use this convention throughout the section.

Local derivative estimates. We recall that the forward-backward pass provides ϕ⁡(0)\phi(0) and the directional derivative, ϕ′​(0)=⟨∇F​(θ),z⟩.\phi^{\prime}(0)=\langle\nabla F(\theta),z\rangle. ZFO adds two symmetric fixed-batch evaluations,

ϕ⁡(ϵ)=F⁡(θ+ϵ​z),and​ϕ​(−ϵ)=F⁡(θ−ϵ​z).\phi(\epsilon)=F(\theta+\epsilon z),\;{\rm and\;}\phi(-\epsilon)=F(\theta-\epsilon z).

We estimate the second directional derivative by the central finite difference

ϕ′′^​(0)=ϕ⁡(ϵ)−2​ϕ​(0)+ϕ⁡(−ϵ)ϵ2.\widehat{\phi^{\prime\prime}}(0)=\frac{\phi(\epsilon)-2\phi(0)+\phi(-\epsilon)}{\epsilon^{2}}.

Using the available first-order derivative, the same two probes also yield

ϕ′′′^​(0)=3ϵ3​(ϕ⁡(ϵ)−ϕ⁡(−ϵ)−2​ϵ​ϕ′​(0)).\widehat{\phi^{\prime\prime\prime}}(0)=\frac{3}{\epsilon^{3}}\left(\phi(\epsilon)-\phi(-\epsilon)-2\epsilon\phi^{\prime}(0)\right).

For compactness, define: a=ϕ′​(0),b=ϕ′′^​(0),a=\phi^{\prime}(0),b=\widehat{\phi^{\prime\prime}}(0), and c=ϕ′′′^​(0).c=\widehat{\phi^{\prime\prime\prime}}(0). ZFO uses these quantities to construct a local approximation of ϕ\phi (see Figure 1), considering both polynomial models derived from Taylor expansions and rational models derived from Padé approximations.

(a) Taylor models. The second-order Taylor model is T2​(s)=ϕ⁡(0)+a​s+12​b​s2.T_{2}(s)=\phi(0)+as+\frac{1}{2}bs^{2}. Since T2T_{2} is quadratic, the maximizer is obtained by checking the endpoints of II and, when feasible, the stationary point s=−a/b.s=-{a}/{b}. Similarly, the third-order Taylor model is T3​(s)=ϕ⁡(0)+a​s+12​b​s2+16​c​s3.T_{3}(s)=\phi(0)+as+\frac{1}{2}bs^{2}+\frac{1}{6}cs^{3}. The candidate maximizers are the endpoints of II and the real roots inside II of a+b​s+12​c​s2=0.a+bs+\frac{1}{2}cs^{2}=0.

(b) Padé models. The Padé variants approximate ϕ\phi using rational functions. The second-order Padé model is

P2​(s)=ϕ⁡(0)+a​s1+q2​s,q2=−b2​a,P_{2}(s)=\phi(0)+\frac{as}{1+q_{2}s},\quad q_{2}=-\frac{b}{2a},

Similarly, the third-order Padé model is

P3​(s)=ϕ⁡(0)+a​s+ρ​s21+q3​s, where ​q3=−c3​b,ρ=b2+a​q3.P_{3}(s)=\phi(0)+\frac{as+\rho s^{2}}{1+q_{3}s},\text{ where }q_{3}=-\frac{c}{3b},\quad\rho=\frac{b}{2}+aq_{3}.

If a Padé denominator has a pole inside II, or if its coefficients are ill-defined, ZFO rejects the Padé step and falls back to the quadratic Taylor step. This safeguard avoids unstable rational extrapolation near singularities.

Model selection and update. Each ZFO variant corresponds to one model choice from {T2,T3,P2,P3}.\{T_{2},T_{3},P_{2},P_{3}\}. For a chosen model MM in this set, ZFO computes the step by solving

sM∈arg⁡maxs∈I⁡M⁡(s).s_{M}\in\arg\max_{s\in I}M(s). (3)

All ZFO variants use the same direction, surrogate, and feasible interval. They differ only in how they convert two additional evaluations into a scalar step length. GeN [9] also fits within this abstraction as a specific quadratic ZFO instance. GeN uses two function evaluations along the first-order direction to construct a generalized Newton step. Our instances reuse the directional derivative already available from the backward pass so that the same two probes recover both second- and third-order directional information and support Taylor and Padé models. GeN uses curvature-based rejection as its safeguard, while the instances studied here optimize over a bounded interval and fall back when a Padé model is ill-defined. ZFO’s novelty is the fixed-budget local-model abstraction, its family of Taylor/Padé instantiations, and the associated unified analysis and empirical validation. Algorithm 1 summarizes our framework.

3 Theoretical Analysis

This section provides a theoretical justification for the ZFO step-selection framework. The analysis has three components. First, we show that shared-batch evaluations yield reliable finite-difference estimates of directional curvature; see §3.1 (i). Second, conditional on the sampled examples, we show that maximizing the local ZFO model returns a step whose objective value is close to the best value attainable over the search interval; see §3.1 (ii). Third, we connect this local step-selection property to a global stationarity guarantee for the ZFO update sequence; see §3.2. We omit the iteration index tt when no ambiguity arises.

3.1 Local Convergence Analysis

Shared-batch common-random-numbers (CRN). ZFO evaluates all local objective values on the same minibatch. At a fixed iteration, the examples are sampled once and then reused across the evaluations {ϕ⁡(−ϵ),ϕ⁡(0),ϕ⁡(ϵ)}.\left\{\phi(-\epsilon),\phi(0),\phi(\epsilon)\right\}. After conditioning on these shared examples, ϕ\phi becomes a deterministic function of the scalar step length, ss. This conditional determinism is the basis of the local approximation analysis. Let τ={τ1,…,τn}\tau=\{\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{n}\} denote the shared sampled examples used under CRN. For each example τi\tau_{i}, define the per-sample directional objective ϕi​(s)=F⁡(θ+s​z,τi).\phi_{i}(s)=F(\theta+sz;\tau_{i}). The empirical shared-batch CRN objective is ϕ⁡(s)=1n​∑i=1nϕi​(s).\phi(s)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi_{i}(s).

Definition 1 (Population directional objective).

The population counterpart of the empirical CRN objective is ψ⁡(s)=𝔼τ​[ϕi​(s)],\psi(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[\phi_{i}(s)], where the expectation is taken with respect to the distribution used to generate the empirical objective.

(i) Local smoothness assumptions. The first group of assumptions ensures that the directional objective admits Taylor expansions with controlled remainders.

Assumption 1 (Pathwise smoothness).

For each example τi\tau_{i}, the per-sample directional objective ϕi\phi_{i} is five times continuously differentiable on the interval [−ϵ,R][-\epsilon,R]: ϕi∈C5​([−ϵ,R]).\phi_{i}\in C^{5}([-\epsilon,R]).

Assumption 2 (Higher-order derivative bounds).

There exist constants W,M,B,L>0W,M,B,L>0 such that, for every ii and every s∈[−ϵ,R]s\in[-\epsilon,R], |ϕi′′​(s)|≤W,|\phi_{i}^{\prime\prime}(s)|\leq W, |ϕi′′′​(s)|≤M,|\phi_{i}^{\prime\prime\prime}(s)|\leq M, |ϕi(4)​(s)|≤B,|\phi_{i}^{(4)}(s)|\leq B, and |ϕi(5)​(s)|≤L.|\phi_{i}^{(5)}(s)|\leq L.

(ii) Sampling assumptions. Population concentration is analyzed at a fixed iterate and direction under the independent-example assumptions below. Algorithm 1 reuses its batch across probes, but also computes the direction from that batch; CRN alone does not establish the independence needed by this concentration argument. Thus Theorem 1 is a fixed-direction result, whereas the approximation guarantee in Theorem 2 is pathwise once the batch and direction are fixed. Bounded directional derivatives imply the sub-Gaussian condition by Hoeffding’s lemma; see (4).

Assumption 3 (CRN).

For each index ii, the same example τi\tau_{i} is used to evaluate {ϕi​(−ϵ),ϕi​(0),ϕi​(ϵ)}.\{\phi_{i}(-\epsilon),\phi_{i}(0),\phi_{i}(\epsilon)\}. Moreover, for i≠ji\neq j, the examples τi\tau_{i} and τj\tau_{j} are sampled independently.

Assumption 4.

(Sub-Gaussian Deviation) For each ϕi,\phi_{i}, the directional deviations at s=0s=0 are sub-gaussian up to third order, i.e., there exists constant σ\sigma such that, for every k∈{0,1,2,3}k\in\{0,1,2,3\} and all λ∈ℝ,\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, 𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ⁡[ϕi(k)​(0)−ψ(k)​(0)])]≤exp⁡(λ2​σ22).\mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda[\phi_{i}^{(k)}(0)-\psi^{(k)}(0)])]\leq\exp(\frac{\lambda^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}).

Theorem 1 (CRN curvature concentration).

Suppose Assumptions 1–4 hold. Then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, |ϕ′′^​(0)−ψ′′​(0)|≤B​ϵ212+σ​2​log⁡(4/δ)n,\left|\widehat{\phi^{\prime\prime}}(0)-\psi^{\prime\prime}(0)\right|\leq\frac{B\epsilon^{2}}{12}+\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\log(4/\delta)}{n}}, and |ϕ′′′^​(0)−ψ′′′​(0)|≤L​ϵ220+σ​2​log⁡(4/δ)n.\left|\widehat{\phi^{\prime\prime\prime}}(0)-\psi^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)\right|\leq\frac{L\epsilon^{2}}{20}+\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\log(4/\delta)}{n}}.

Theorem 1 shows that the finite-difference curvature estimates used by ZFO concentrate around their population counterparts. Each bound contains two terms. The first term is a deterministic finite-difference bias controlled by the perturbation scale ϵ\epsilon and the relevant higher-order derivative bound. The second term is a stochastic sampling term that decreases at the classic rate 1/n1/\sqrt{n}. Thus, under CRN, the two additional objective evaluations provide statistically meaningful curvature information.

After conditioning on the shared examples, the empirical objective ϕ\phi is deterministic. Let sM∈arg⁡maxs∈[0,R]​T2​(s)s_{M}\in\arg\max_{s\in[0,R]}T_{2}(s) denote the model-selected step by T2T_{2}, and let sϕ∈arg⁡maxs∈[0,R]⁡ϕ⁡(s)s_{\phi}\in\arg\max_{s\in[0,R]}\phi(s) denote the best step for the empirical CRN objective over the same interval.

Theorem 2 (Second-order Taylor approximation bound).

Suppose Assumptions 1 and 2 hold. Then the step selected by maximizing the second-order Taylor model satisfies ϕ⁡(sM)≥ϕ⁡(sϕ)−M​R33−B​ϵ2​R212.\phi(s_{M})\geq\phi(s_{\phi})-\frac{MR^{3}}{3}-\frac{B\epsilon^{2}R^{2}}{12}.

Theorem 2 shows that, once the examples are fixed, ZFO selects a step that is close to the best step available in the search interval. The first error term, M​R33,\frac{MR^{3}}{3}, is the deterministic Taylor approximation error over the interval. The second error term, B​ϵ2​R212,\frac{B\epsilon^{2}R^{2}}{12}, is the error caused by estimating curvature through finite differences. The guarantee is strongest when the search radius RR is moderate, the perturbation scale ϵ\epsilon is small, and the directional objective has limited higher-order variation. The same proof strategy extends to the third-order Taylor model. For the Padé variants, the local model is rational rather than polynomial. These models can better capture nonlinear curvature changes over a finite interval. Their approximation guarantees follow from the same maximizer-comparison argument, replacing the Taylor remainder by a rational residual term. We defer the analysis of these variants to §B.1.

3.2 Global convergence Analysis

We now connect the local analysis to the true optimization objective JJ. Recall that ZFO optimizes on the surrogate Ft,F_{t}, whose expectation under the current sampling distribution is F¯t​(θ+s​zt)=ψ⁡(s)\bar{F}_{t}(\theta+sz_{t})=\psi(s). For instance, standard policy optimization [53] and its modern extensions [45, 46] construct surrogates such that ∇J​(θt)=∇F¯​(θt)\nabla J(\theta_{t})=\nabla\bar{F}(\theta_{t}) at the current-iterate. Define the expected directional alignment quantity qt=𝔼⁡[⟨∇J​(θt),zt⟩].q_{t}=\mathbb{E}[\langle\nabla J(\theta_{t}),z_{t}\rangle]. We start by stating two main classical assumptions that we use in the sequel.

Assumption 5 (Smooth and bounded objective).

The true objective J:ℝd→ℝJ:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is ℒJ\mathcal{L}_{J}-smooth and bounded above by J⋆J^{\star}. That is, for all x,yx,y, J⁡(y)≥J⁡(x)+⟨∇J​(x),y−x⟩−ℒJ2​‖y−x‖2,J(y)\geq J(x)+\langle\nabla J(x),y-x\rangle-\frac{\mathcal{L}_{J}}{2}\|y-x\|^{2}, and J⁡(θt)≤J⋆J(\theta_{t})\leq J^{\star} for all iterations tt. Additionally, the expected surrogate F¯\bar{F} is also ℒF¯\mathcal{L}_{\bar{F}}-smooth.

Assumption 6 (Aligned update direction).

There exists μ>0\mu>0 such that, for all tt, qt=𝔼t​[⟨∇J​(θt),zt⟩]≥μ​‖∇J​(θt)‖.q_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle\nabla J(\theta_{t}),z_{t}\rangle]\geq\mu\|\nabla J(\theta_{t})\|.

Assumption 6 is natural since gradient methods estimate an ascent direction for the objective [46]. Although optimizers such as AdamW rescale this direction, the resulting update remains positively oriented with ∇J​(θt)\nabla J(\theta_{t}) in expectation [3], supporting the assumption of μ>0\mu>0.

We start with a Lemma that bounds the step-selection error at iteration tt of the objective: maxs∈It⁡J⁡(θt+s​zt)−J⁡(θt+st​zt).\max_{s\in I_{t}}J(\theta_{t}+sz_{t})-J(\theta_{t}+s_{t}z_{t}). This quantity measures the loss in objective value by using the ZFO-selected step sts_{t} instead of the best step available in the interval ItI_{t} for the true objective JJ.

Lemma 1 (Surrogate vs. Empirical Difference).

Let Assumptions 1-5 hold, then maxs∈It⁡J⁡(θt+s​zt)−J⁡(θt+st​zt)≤Δt,\max_{s\in I_{t}}J(\theta_{t}+sz_{t})-J(\theta_{t}+s_{t}z_{t})\leq\Delta_{t}, holds with probability at least 1−δ,1-\delta, where

Δt≔(ℒJ+ℒF¯)​Rt2+2​σ​(1+Rt)​2​log⁡(4/δ)n+2​W​Rt2+ϕ⁡(sϕ)−ϕ⁡(sM).\Delta_{t}\coloneq(\mathcal{L}_{J}+\mathcal{L}_{\bar{F}})R_{t}^{2}+2\sigma(1+R_{t})\sqrt{\frac{2\log(4/\delta)}{n}}+2WR_{t}^{2}+\phi(s_{\phi})-\phi(s_{M}).

This lemma quantifies the loss in objective value when the ZFO step sts_{t}, selected through the local model, is used instead of the best step in the interval ItI_{t}. The error term Δt\Delta_{t} combines smoothness mismatch, finite-sample concentration error, approximation error, and the model-selection gap ϕ⁡(sϕ)−ϕ⁡(sM)\phi(s_{\phi})-\phi(s_{M}). E.g., when the local model is the second-order Taylor model T2T_{2}, using Theorem 2 we get

Δt≤(ℒJ+ℒF¯)​Rt2+2​σ​(1+Rt)​2​log⁡(4/δ)n+2​W​Rt2+M​R33+B​ϵ2​R212.\Delta_{t}\leq(\mathcal{L}_{J}+\mathcal{L}_{\bar{F}})R_{t}^{2}+2\sigma(1+R_{t})\sqrt{\frac{2\log(4/\delta)}{n}}+2WR_{t}^{2}+\frac{MR^{3}}{3}+\frac{B\epsilon^{2}R^{2}}{12}.

Finally, Theorem 3 converts the local quality of the ZFO step-selection rule into a global stationarity guarantee.

Theorem 3 (Stationarity of the ZFO update).

Let Assumptions 5–6 hold and qt/ℒJ∈It.q_{t}/\mathcal{L}_{J}\in I_{t}. Then, for every T>0T>0, with probability at least 1−δ,1-\delta, we have

min0≤t≤T⁡𝔼​‖∇J​(θt)‖2≤2​ℒJ​(J⋆−J⁡(θ0))μ2​T+2​ℒJ​Δ~Tμ2, where ​Δ~T=1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡[Δt].\min_{0\leq t\leq T}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla J(\theta_{t})\|^{2}\leq\frac{2\mathcal{L}_{J}(J^{\star}-J(\theta_{0}))}{\mu^{2}T}+\frac{2\mathcal{L}_{J}\tilde{\Delta}_{T}}{\mu^{2}},\text{ where }\tilde{\Delta}_{T}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}].

The upper bound in Theorem 3 has two terms. The first term, 2​ℒJ​(J⋆−J⁡(θ0))μ2​T,\frac{2\mathcal{L}_{J}(J^{\star}-J(\theta_{0}))}{\mu^{2}T}, is the usual optimization term and decays at rate 1/T1/T. The second term, 2​ℒJ​Δ~Tμ2,\frac{2\mathcal{L}_{J}\tilde{\Delta}_{T}}{\mu^{2}}, is the price paid for imperfect step selection. Thus, ZFO does not necessarily converge exactly to a stationary point unless the average step-selection error vanishes. Instead, it converges to a neighborhood of stationarity whose size is controlled by the error Δ¯T.\bar{\Delta}_{T}.

The three results establish the theoretical foundation of ZFO. The CRN concentration theorem establishes the statistical reliability of the finite-difference curvature estimates; the deterministic approximation theorem shows that maximizing the ZFO model yields a near-optimal local step; and the global stationarity theorem shows that controlled step-selection error preserves convergence to stationarity. Together, these results justify the central mechanism of ZFO: a small number of fixed-batch objective evaluations can recover useful local curvature information and improve step selection over a fixed first-order update while retaining a principled convergence interpretation.

4 Experiments

Organization of the Results. We organize our experimental results as follows: In the main paper, (i) we compare ZFO against first-order fine-tuning with AdamW and zeroth-order fine-tuning with MeZO across several LLMs and datasets in Table 1; (ii) we conduct a focused Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B sub-study over additional reasoning benchmarks in Table 2; (iii) we evaluate ZFO on classical optimization problems to assess its benefits beyond LLM fine-tuning in Figure 2; (iv) we summarize the ablation studies in the appendix; and (v) we report wall-clock and memory overheads in Figures 3 and 4 to quantify the computational cost of ZFO. We defer the remaining experiments and expanded diagnostics to the Appendix C.2, where (vi) we provide the complete six-problem classical optimization study in Table 8 and Figure 5, (vii) we validate the local ZFO approximants on analytical functions in Figure 6 and the step-selection mechanism on controlled toy RLVR environments in Figure 7, (viii) we provide learning-rate sensitivity curves in Figure 8 and study the interaction between α\alpha and β\beta in Figure 9, including the complementary β=1\beta=1 control in Table 12, (ix) we analyze the frequency of the steps selected by each ZFO method in Table 13, (x) we summarize cross-setting improvements in Table 9 and compare against additional first-order baselines (Prodigy [37] and AdamW [31]) in Table 10, and (xi) we evaluate the sequential ZFO-Seq against line-search baselines (Armijo [39], BB [4], Polyak [42], and PLS [33]) in Table 11. Unless otherwise stated, all reported results are averaged over three seeds. The LLM experiments use the implementation described in §C.1.1. Additional experimental configuration details are provided in §C.1.2.

RLVR, LLMs, and Datasets used for Fine-tuning. We report the performance of various high-dimensional models configured for an RLVR setup using the GRPO policy gradient [47] and the AdamW optimizer [31], including Qwen-2.5-MATH-1.5B [54], Phi-2 [24], Gemma-2-2B [52], and Llama-3.2-1B [19] on the datasets GSM8K [12], SVAMP [41], AsDiv [35], OpenBookQA [36], and a (512/256 train/evaluation) subset of MATH [21]; Table 3 summarizes the model and dataset details.

Learning rate scheduler. For a fair comparison, we fix the learning rate α\alpha to the value that performs the best for the FO baseline, chosen from the set {10−6,5×10−6,10−5}\{10^{-6},5\times 10^{-6},10^{-5}\}, and consequently select the best bound β\beta from {3,5,10}\{3,5,10\}; the remainder of the configuration details are in §C.1.2.

4.1 ZFO for LLM fine-tuning and classic optimization

(i) Does directional ZO step selection improve FO optimization? We show the performance of the ZFO framework on LLM fine-tuning in Table 1, where at least one ZFO variant improves on the first-order fine-tuning (FO FT) baseline for every model-dataset pair, indicating that ZFO’s benefits are not confined to a single model family or benchmark. We observe the largest gains where the FO baseline is relatively weak or highly variable, including SVAMP for Phi-2 and Gemma-2-2B, as well as AsDiv for Llama and MATH and OpenBookQA for Qwen. When the FO baseline is already strong, such as Qwen on SVAMP, ZFO yields smaller but still positive improvements in mean performance. Although the best-performing ZFO variant changes across tasks and models, Padé3 provides a strong representative instance of the framework, improving over FO in 14 of the 16 LLM settings summarized in Table 9. Padé3 is a strong representative default in our experiments, although the preferred local model remains task-dependent.

(ii) Qwen Sub-Study. Table 2 extends the main results by isolating Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B on four reasoning benchmarks: ARC-Challenge [11], StrategyQA [15], FOLIO [20], and CODAH [10]. At least one ZFO method outperforms the FT baseline on every dataset, with the largest improvements on ARC-Challenge (↑\uparrow8.818.81 over FO FT) and CODAH (↑\uparrow4.924.92 over FO FT). Even under the best learning rate configurations, the main results and the Qwen sub-study indicate that FO FT exhibits seed variance under our settings.

(iii) Classic Optimization. To show that ZFO is not intrinsically tied to RLVR and to examine ZFO’s performance beyond LLM fine-tuning, Figure 2 presents three classic optimization problems; see Table 8 for the comprehensive summary of the six classic optimization problems. At least one ZFO variant achieves a substantially lower median objective than its corresponding FO baseline on every displayed problem after 100 updates. Taylor3–AdamW yields the strongest results on nonlinear least squares and Beale, while Padé3–AdamW performs best on Rosenbrock. Consistent with our LLM experiments, the best approximant varies across problems, indicating that the gains from step selection depend on the local objective.

(iv) Ablation Studies. We provide additional ablation studies in Appendix C.2 to better understand when and how ZFO improves step selection. Figure 8 compares ZFO against AdamW across fixed learning rates, showing that gains in Table 1 cannot generally be recovered by simply changing the FO learning rate. Figure 9 further studies the interaction between the learning rate α\alpha and search bound β\beta, where increasing β\beta is generally beneficial at smaller learning rates but can become unstable once α\alpha is large, showing that the two parameters are complementary but not interchangeable. Figure 7 provides a clear β=1\beta=1 control. Table 13 shows that the four ZFO instances use the search interval differently, ranging from primarily interior steps for Taylor3 to mostly endpoint decisions for Padé2.

4.2 Computational Cost

The relative computational overhead of ZFO is small. A standard iteration involves 4 key components: a rollout call for the trajectory τt,\tau_{t}, a reward evaluation R⁡(τt)R(\tau_{t}), a forward pass, and a backward pass. In contrast, our ZFO methods leave all 4 operations untouched and only call two additional forward-pass probes. Since these probes are only forward passes, the overhead is small and comparable to the forward-only cost structure of ZO methods such as MeZO [34]. From this perspective, we present both wall-clock time costs in Figure 3 and memory overhead costs in Figure 4. We train the models on an NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU.

Figure 3 decomposes per-iteration runtime for Qwen-2.5-MATH-1.5B on the benchmarks reported in Table 1. ZFO adds ∼5.2%\sim 5.2\% relative wall-clock overhead in this configuration; ZFO incurs real memory overhead.

Figure 4 reports peak GPU memory across three model–dataset pairs, alongside a per-phase breakdown for Qwen-2.5-MATH-1.5B. The overhead ranges from 11.0% (Qwen/GSM8K) to 19.1% (Phi-2/OpenBookQA). We attribute this range to configuration differences; ZFO probes are absorbed with a smaller relative increase, whereas configurations with a small fixed group size and a larger batch see the overhead grow more. The memory allocation panel shows that the dominant cost remains the reference forward pass, while storing the update direction and applying the final blend sit below the existing bottleneck; hence, ZFO does not introduce a new peak; it widens the existing one. We note that the memory-saving trick MeZO relies on does not transfer here, since our update direction is the FO gradient rather than a random direction.

5 Limitations, Discussion, and Conclusion

What can two probes recover? The backward pass already supplies the local slope; two symmetric probes add estimates of curvature and its variation. Theorem 2 translates local-model error into a bound on the value lost relative to the best step in II. A wider interval permits larger updates but increases approximation error. Bounds and Padé fallbacks limit extrapolation and avoid poles, but do not guarantee that every step improves the surrogate. Theorem 3 then connects step-selection accuracy to convergence. Under the stated assumptions, ZFO therefore retains a stationarity guarantee even with approximate steps.

Padé2 Behavior. Padé2 provides a useful diagnostic because, as shown in the toy validation in §C, it behaves the most like FO since its updates select the endpoint of the search region unless a pole is detected, in which case it falls back to Taylor2. This makes Padé2 a conservative reference for distinguishing whether ZFO gains come from expanding the search region alone or intelligent step selection. In Tables 1 and 2, the richer surrogates frequently outperform Padé2 (e.g., Qwen on MATH, ARC-Challenge, and CODAH). Conversely, when Padé2 improves over FO, then the increased search region contributes in beneficial ways that are not obtainable simply by scaling α.\alpha.

Beyond the Four Instances. We view Taylor2, Taylor3, Padé2, and Padé3 as initial ZFO instances rather than the strongest possible realizations of the framework. Each method is a simple analytic model built from lightweight probes, yet these lightweight probes already yield measurable gains in evaluation performance and training stability across several benchmarks. The main opportunity ZFO provides is not limited to the specific empirical gains reported in this paper, but instead lies in the observation that a meaningful curvature signal can be extracted along the FO direction at low additional cost.

Conclusion. Step-size selection is a classic problem in large-scale optimization. The direction selected by a first-order optimizer is valuable, but the step length remains uncertain. We show that two additional function evaluations along that direction are sufficient to construct useful local models of the one-dimensional objective. This creates a general fixed-query step-selection framework, ZFO. In contrast to ZO methods, ZFO does not estimate a gradient with zeroth-order queries; it estimates how the objective changes along a gradient direction whose orientation has already been supplied by a first-order optimizer.

Existing methods have already explored function-based step selection along a first-order direction, most notably GeN. Our contribution elevates this idea from a single-step rule to a fixed-query directional modeling framework—the same two probes can support multiple local models, including higher-order Taylor and rational Padé approximations, while the analysis separates finite-difference estimation error, local-model approximation error, and global optimization error. Therefore, ZFO is not primarily a new Taylor or Padé step-size formula. It is a fixed-query framework for exploiting zeroth-order information along an already trusted first-order direction, together with a theory that explains the statistical and optimization error introduced by this separation. In that sense, GeN is a special case of the broader ZFO abstraction, rather than an unrelated baseline. In the same spirit, we encourage the practitioners to add their favorite functional approximators to the ZFO framework.

Across our experiments, ZFO often improves step selection over the fixed FO update. The quality of the selected step remains dependent on the local model, search radius, and alignment of the underlying first-order direction.

Organization. We organize the Appendix as follows: In Section A, we detail the related work. In Section B, we quote the general assumptions and provide detailed proofs of our theoretical result in the main paper. Finally, in Section C, we discuss the configuration details for our experiments in §C.1 and provide additional performance insights in §C.2.

Appendix A Related work

We position ZFO within three lines of work that motivate or contrast with our approach. Together, these related works inspire ZFO’s central premise that cheap query calls can help model local objective behavior along the gradient direction.

Policy Optimization Stability & Update Regulation. Stability in policy optimization has motivated a range of update-regulation strategies. In policy optimization, methods such as TRPO [45] enforce a KL-constrained trust region, while PPO [46] replaces explicit constraints with a clipped surrogate objective to stabilize updates. More recent approaches, such as GRPO [47], further emphasize that training stability is highly sensitive to the way policy updates are regulated. Related works also consider wrapper-based stabilization strategies for policy-gradient methods that regulate whether an update should be accepted [1]. Our work is motivated by the same stability concern; however, we approach it from a different perspective by explicitly modeling the objective along the update direction path.

Zeroth-Order Optimization. Our work is also related to ZO optimization for fine-tuning large language models. Methods such as MeZO and CARS use central finite differences along random directions to approximate gradient or curvature behavior [34, 26]; particularly, MeZO uses finite differences along random directions to approximate the gradient, and CARS uses a second-order finite difference to approximate the Hessian. Extensions of MeZO include curvature, sparsity, and query-efficient estimators. Hi-ZOO incorporates a diagonal Hessian estimate at the cost of an extra forward pass [56]. Sparse-MeZO restricts updates to noise-resistant weights to enable larger step sizes [29]. GraCe leverages gradient sparsity to achieve a dependence on dimension in query complexity [44]. HiSo carries Hessian-informed ZO into the federated setting [28]. Complementary benchmarking has mapped the landscape of ZO optimizers across fine-tuning paradigms [55]. Recent theoretical work further establishes that ZO optimization is equivalent to single-step policy optimization [43], suggesting a natural connection between zeroth-order methods and RLVR that ZFO exploits.

Line-Search & Adaptive Step Size. Broadly, our method is similar to line-search and adaptive learning-rate methods, including Polyak step size [42], Barzilai-Borwein [4], and stochastic variants such as Probabilistic line-search [33] and Stochastic Armijo line-search [40]. These approaches adapt step sizes by repeatedly evaluating candidate points along a univariate objective, often requiring multiple queries. In contrast, our method uses only two symmetric probes to approximately recover higher-order directional information to construct a local model of the objective. This results in a fixed-budget alternative to classical line-search methods.

Generalized Newton Step Selection. Among closely related recent methods, generalized Newton step selection or GeN [9] has already explored function-based step selection along a first-order direction, providing an early example of combining FO directions with low-query step-size adaptation. Our contribution is to elevate this idea from a single-step rule to a fixed-query directional modeling framework: the same two probes can support multiple local models, including higher-order Taylor and rational Padé approximations, while the analysis separates finite-difference estimation error, local-model approximation error, and global optimization error. GeN is a special case of the broader ZFO abstraction, rather than an unrelated baseline.

Appendix B Addendum to Theoretical Analysis

This section provides the theoretical foundations needed to characterize when, why, and how ZFO can reliably improve step selection. We first establish concentration guarantees for the finite-difference curvature estimates, then bound how closely the resulting models recover the best step within their local interval, and we finally connect these local guarantees to global stationarity of the ZFO update. Together, these results separate the sources of error introduced by stochastic estimation, local function approximation, and step selection, providing a theoretical justification for the mechanisms used by ZFO.

To justify using finite-difference curvature information for ZFO step selection, we first ask whether the second- and third-order directional derivatives estimated from a shared batch can reliably approximate their population counterparts.

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ⁡(X−𝔼⁡[X]))]≤exp⁡(λ2​(b−a)28),for​all​λ∈ℝ.\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\lambda(X-\mathbb{E}[X])\right)\right]\leq\exp\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}(b-a)^{2}}{8}\right),\qquad{\rm for\;all\;}\lambda\in\mathbb{R}. (4)

Thus, every bounded random variable is sub-Gaussian with parameter σ=(b−a)/2\sigma=(b-a)/2.

Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} be independent sub-Gaussian random variables with parameter σ>0\sigma>0, i.e.,

𝔼⁡[eλ​Xi]≤eλ2​σ2/2,∀λ∈ℝ.\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\lambda X_{i}}\right]\leq e^{\lambda^{2}\sigma^{2}/2},\quad\forall\lambda\in\mathbb{R}.

ℙ⁡(|1n​∑i=1nXi|≤σ​2​log⁡(2/ζ)n)≥1−ζ.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\right|\leq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2/\zeta)}{n}}\right)\geq 1-\zeta. (5)

Additional Model Error Bounds. To understand how accurately ZFO’s local models can choose a step, we next ask how much objective value may be lost when maximizing a finite-difference Taylor or Padé approximation. The proof technique used in Theorem 2 generalizes naturally to higher-order ZFO models. This allows us to characterize the approximation gap of Taylor3 and Padé over the search region [0,R].[0,{R}]. Corollary 1 establishes a similar bound for Taylor3 as Theorem 2 did for Taylor2. Corollaries 2 and 3 adapt a similar structure through the residual r⁡(s)≔D⁡(s)​ϕ​(s)−N⁡(s).r(s)\coloneqq D(s)\phi(s)-N(s). All three results yield finite-difference and model truncation errors.

Padé3 alternative forms. Third-order matching does not uniquely determine the Padé form, since the numerator and denominator degrees can be allocated differently. The construction above uses a quadratic numerator and linear denominator, corresponding to a 2/12/1 approximant. Below, we consider the complementary 1/21/2 form, with a linear numerator and quadratic denominator, which is also used in our LLM experiments. Both constructions match the local expansion through third order under their respective nondegeneracy conditions, but generally produce different performance curves. These choices illustrate the flexibility of ZFO’s rational surrogate construction.

Together, these three corollaries and Theorem 2 quantify how the additional curvature information used by ZFO models affects the worst-case approximation gap. The Taylor3 bound replaces the 𝒪⁡(R3)\mathcal{O}({R}^{3}) term in Theorem 2 with an 𝒪⁡(R4)\mathcal{O}({R}^{4}) term. Hence the relationship between the errors of Taylor2 and Taylor3 can be most significantly characterized by the power of their search regions R.{R}. The Padé2 bound remains closer in order to the Taylor2 bound, but introduces the residual-controlled Q​R33​η\frac{QR^{3}}{3\eta} term. The Padé3 bound exhibits a similar 𝒪⁡(R4)\mathcal{O}({R}^{4}) term as Taylor3 and also uses a residual error term. Overall, the two corollaries reinforce the same conclusion as Theorem 2; when the search region is moderate and the perturbation scale is small, then ZFO maximizers achieve values close to the best step within a local trust region.

ZFO Dominance. The following theorem is referenced in the main text as an appendix result. As a supplementary result beyond the main-text analysis, we next ask whether the ZFO-selected Taylor2 step can be guaranteed to perform at least as well as the original first-order step under suitable local curvature conditions.

Under Assumption 1 and Assumptions 9-11, we compare the Taylor2 step with the typical FO step by bounding the curvature approximation error, imposing strong concavity on [0,R][0,{R}], and requiring the Taylor-model maximizer to be an interior point. B.2 ZFO Global Stationarity

To connect the local ZFO step-selection guarantees to overall optimization behavior, we finally ask whether repeatedly applying these approximate directional steps still drives the training process toward a stationary point of the population objective.

ZFO is computed on the sampled surrogate Ft​(θ)=F⁡(θ,St)F_{t}(\theta)=F(\theta;S_{t}), where StS_{t} is generated at the current iterate θt\theta_{t} and then fixed for nearby perturbations. We define the expected surrogate obtained under the current sampling distribution F¯t​(θ)≔𝔼S​[F⁡(θ,S)]\bar{F}_{t}(\theta)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{S}[F(\theta;S)]. In our theoretical analysis, the true objective JJ and the expected surrogate F¯t\bar{F}_{t} have the same gradient ∇F¯t​(θ)=∇J​(θt)\nabla\bar{F}_{t}(\theta)=\nabla J(\theta_{t}). In this formulation FtF_{t} is used for parameter updates, while its expectation F¯t\bar{F}_{t} develops a reliable objective signal.

Appendix C Addendum to Experimental Results

This addendum collects supplementary diagnostics that complement the main results. We first validate the ZFO step-selection mechanism on two low-dimensional toy RLVR environments, then discuss the local-approximation behavior of each ZFO method on a panel of analytic test functions, and finally report cross-setting win ratios that summarize how consistently each variant improves over the FO baseline.

C.1 Configuration

This section specifies the objective and implementation choices used throughout our experiments. First, we define the GRPO surrogate, optimized by each method, then report the hyperparameter configurations used for the main large-model runs, Qwen sub-study, and toy validation.

C.1.1 Surrogate Objective Formulation

GRPO Surrogate. For this paper, the surrogate FtF_{t} instantiates the GRPO objective. Let 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} denote the set of prompts in the current batch, with |𝒫t||\mathcal{P}_{t}| the batch size and GG the number of examples sampled per prompt. For each prompt i∈{1,…,|𝒫t|}i\in\{1,\ldots,|\mathcal{P}_{t}|\} and each sampled example j∈{1,…,G}j\in\{1,\ldots,G\}, let τi,j,t\tau_{i,j,t} denote the sampled example, |τi,j,t||\tau_{i,j,t}| its length, and (xi,j,v,yi,j,v)(x_{i,j,v},y_{i,j,v}) the state-action pair at token position vv. The surrogate is

Ft(θ;St)=1|𝒫t|​G∑i=1|𝒫t|∑j=1GA~i,j,tlogπθ(τi,j,t)−κ⋅KL(πθ∥πref),F_{t}(\theta;S_{t})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{t}|G}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{P}_{t}|}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\widetilde{A}_{i,j,t}\log\pi_{\theta}(\tau_{i,j,t})-\kappa\cdot\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\rm ref}),

where κ>0\kappa>0 is the KL coefficient, A~i,j,t\widetilde{A}_{i,j,t} is the group-relative advantage given as

A~i,j,t=ρ⁡(τi,j,t)−1G​∑k=1Gρ⁡(τi,k,t),\widetilde{A}_{i,j,t}=\rho(\tau_{i,j,t})-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{k=1}^{G}\rho(\tau_{i,k,t}),

and ρ\rho is the verifiable reward given by

ρ⁡(τi,j,t)=𝟙τi,j,t∈𝒞t,\rho(\tau_{i,j,t})=\mathds{1}_{\tau_{i,j,t}\in\mathcal{C}_{t}},

with 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} denoting the set of sampled examples deemed correct by the verifier at iteration tt. The KL penalty is computed at the token level and averaged across the batch:

KL(πθ∥πref)=1|𝒫t|​G∑i=1|𝒫t|∑j=1G1|τi,j,t|∑v=1|τi,j,t|[logπθ(yi,j,v∣xi,j,v)−logπref(yi,j,v∣xi,j,v)].\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\rm ref})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{t}|G}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{P}_{t}|}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\tau_{i,j,t}|}\sum_{v=1}^{|\tau_{i,j,t}|}\bigl[\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,j,v}\mid x_{i,j,v})-\log\pi_{\rm ref}(y_{i,j,v}\mid x_{i,j,v})\bigr].

Implementation-Level Interpretation of α\alpha and β\beta. In the theory, we describe the ZFO search interval using the effective radius Rt=β​sFOR_{t}=\beta s_{\rm FO}, where sFOs_{\rm FO} represents the scale of the base first-order step. Conceptually, this makes the learning rate α\alpha and the bound β\beta nearly interchangeable as step-scale controls. Under an idealized linear scaling view, replacing (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) with another pair having the same product α​β\alpha\beta would therefore produce a comparable search radius.

In implementation, however, the two quantities enter at different stages. The base optimizer first forms its tentative AdamW update using learning rate α\alpha. If θt\theta_{t} is the parameter vector before this tentative update and θ^t\widehat{\theta}_{t} is the parameter vector after it, then the realized optimizer displacement is

dt=θ^t−θt.d_{t}=\widehat{\theta}_{t}-\theta_{t}.

ZFO then searches along this displacement through parameters θt+a​dt\theta_{t}+ad_{t} with a∈[0,β]a\in[0,\beta]. Thus the implemented effective search radius is Rt=β​‖dt‖R_{t}=\beta\|d_{t}\|.

Therefore, matched-product pairs such as (α,β)=(10−6,5)(\alpha,\beta)=(10^{-6},5) and (5×10−6,1)(5\times 10^{-6},1) should be understood as equivalent in nominal search scale, but not necessarily identical in implementation. They can produce different results because α\alpha affects the optimizer displacement dtd_{t} before ZFO constructs its search line.

LLM implementation. GRPO supplies the optimizer direction and first-order coefficient. Symmetric probes evaluate a separate reward-minus-KL score on fixed sampled sequences, with rewards held constant. The probe values and GRPO slope jointly define the local model used for step selection. The theory analyzes an idealized ZFO setting in which the directional derivative and function probes are evaluations of the same sampled surrogate. The RLVR implementation approximates this setting by holding sampled responses and rewards fixed during the probes.

C.1.2 Empirical Configurations

All large-model runs share the fixed hyperparameters listed in Table 4. We hold these values constant so that observed differences in performance can be attributed to the update method as opposed to incidental variance in sampling, regularization, or optimization settings. Each reported result is averaged over the three seeds {100,101,102},\{100,101,102\}, and the standard deviations reported in Tables 1 and  2 are based on these various runs.

We evaluate the models after each epoch, and all runs use the same early-stopping rule; we terminate the training when evaluation accuracy is unchanged for three consecutive epochs. Otherwise, we continue training until the maximum epoch count specified for the corresponding configuration. Per-run hyperparameters differ across model-dataset pairs and include the learning rate α\alpha, the bound hyperparameter β,\beta, and the selected configuration from Table 5. We summarize four configuration types in Table 5 and represent a performance-versus-cost trade-off. Config a is the default, with the largest group size and longest context length. Configs b–d are progressively cheaper alternatives selected when a is infeasible based on either memory or time constraints. Config b reduces both batch and group sizes for memory-constrained runs, c trades group size for a larger batch when throughput is more valuable than rollout diversity, and d additionally shortens the context and reduces epochs.

These per-run details are reported in Table 6 for the main results, including the FO learning rate, ZO learning rate, and each ZFO bound β\beta. The FO learning rate is selected from the sweep {\{1e-6, 5e-6, 1e-5 }\}, and the corresponding bound for each ZFO method is then chosen from a validated sweep over {3,5,10}\{3,5,10\}. The ZO learning rate is tuned independently from the sweep {1e−8,5e−8,1e−7,5e−7}1e-8,5e-8,1e-7,5e-7\}, since ZO methods generally require a smaller effective step scale than FO updates. The performance reported is the mean verifiable reward on the evaluation set. The Qwen sub-study from Table 2 follows a similar protocol but fixes config c across runs (a memory-conservative choice given the sub-study sweeps over four datasets), restricts the learning rate sweep to {\{5e-6, 1e-5 }\}, and limits the bound sweep to {3,5}.\{3,5\}. The Qwen sub-study configurations are reported in Table 7.

The toy models in Figure 7 use a lightweight configuration designed to validate the ZFO step-selection mechanism in a controlled low-dimensional setting. Both environments share a context dimension of 6, a sequence length of 4, and a two-layer policy network of hidden width 48. Each run uses a dataset of 200 contexts trained for 50 steps with batch size 1616, group size G=4G=4, perturbation scale ϵ=10−2,\epsilon=10^{-2}, and KL coefficient of 0.1. The bound hyperparameter β\beta is fixed to 1, so the ZFO search interval collapses to the FO typical step.

Table 3 depicts the models and datasets used throughout our large-model experiments, along with their corresponding parameter counts and dataset sizes. We consider models ranging from 1.23B to 2.7B parameters across a diverse set of mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and knowledge-based benchmarks. We additionally report the datasets used in our Qwen sub-study to provide a complete summary of the main experimental settings considered.

Our MeZO baseline uses a forward-only, two-sided finite-difference update along an unnormalized Gaussian perturbation direction. At each iteration, sampled responses, group-centered reward advantages, and reference-policy log probabilities are held fixed across the positive and negative perturbations. The evaluated objective combines advantage-weighted completion log probabilities with a nonnegative k3k_{3} KL penalty, averaged over completion tokens within each sequence. Both terms use completion-only masking, and responses are decoded from the end of the padded prompt. Objective evaluations run in evaluation mode, with log-ratio clipping for numerical stability. The perturbation direction is regenerated from the same random seed for both probes and the parameter update, avoiding backpropagation.

C.2 Additional Insights

Optimization Beyond Neural Network Training. To evaluate whether ZFO extends beyond neural network optimization, we consider six classical optimization problems: linear least squares, nonlinear least squares, logistic regression, low-rank matrix factorization, Rosenbrock, and Beale. A summary of the problems can be found in Table 8. We evaluate Taylor2, Taylor3, Padé2, and Padé3 with both SGD and AdamW-style directions, alongside their first-order baselines and GeN [9] and present the results in Figure 5. Every method receives an independent search over the 18 learning rates, {1,2,5}×10−5,…,0\{1,2,5\}\times 10^{-5,\ldots,0}, while ZFO methods use a fixed bound β=3\beta=3 and perturbation radius ϵ=10−3\epsilon=10^{-3}. GeN uses γ=0.9\gamma=0.9 and Φ=1\Phi=1 for fair comparison against the ZFO methods. Each experiment runs for 100 gradient updates over three seeds.

The results show that ZFO’s benefits are substantial but depend on both the local model and direction. Taylor3–AdamW attains the lowest final median objectives on nonlinear least squares and Beale, whereas Padé3–AdamW performs best on Rosenbrock. Several ZFO and GeN variants also accelerate matrix factorization relative to ordinary SGD. On linear least squares, most adaptive methods improve moderately over their corresponding first-order baselines, whereas logistic regression converges to essentially the same objective across methods. Some combinations also stall or underperform, particularly on the nonconvex objectives. Thus, the experiment supports ZFO’s applicability beyond LLMs and its ability to yield order-of-magnitude improvements in favorable geometries.

All Roads Lead to ϕ\phi. Figure 6 examines the four ZFO surrogates, Taylor2, Taylor3, Padé2, and Padé3, on a panel of locally analytic functions. In each panel, f⁡(x0)f(x_{0}) and f′​(x0)f^{\prime}(x_{0}) are computed exactly, while the second and third derivatives are approximated by the same finite differences discussed in this paper. The top row consists of functions that are either sub-linear or polynomial on a tight interval; hence the approximations are nearly indistinguishable from the actual function. The bottom row deliberately widens the window by introducing functions that do not have sub-linear properties. Across both rows, the consistent takeaway is that all four interpolants generally agree with a bit of variance on super-polynomial functions.

Toy Model Validation. We first validate the ZFO framework on two low-dimensional toy RLVR environments shown in Figure 7. The first toy model, Grouped Sequence Bandit, is a sequence-decision task that requires a learning algorithm to choose a short sequence of tokens to match a hidden target sequence. Specifically, the model samples a complete sequence based on a small input and updates the parameters based on the reward feedback. The second model, Grouped Path-Matching, uses a similar idea, but makes the reward structure more dependent on the entire sequence path. Instead of rewarding independent tokens, the policy receives a higher reward when its sampled actions remain aligned with the hidden target path. Both environments use a stochastic policy trained with grouped advantages and KL regularization against a frozen reference, replicating the surrogate structure of Ft​(θ,𝒮t)F_{t}(\theta;\mathcal{S}_{t}) used in our larger experiments. Each method is averaged over 5 seeds with the bound hyperparameter β=1\beta=1; the remainder of the configuration can be found in §C.1.2.

Figure 7 reports the training curves and final performance across both environments. Across both toy environments, the ZFO methods improve over the FO and ZO baselines, supporting the central claim that additional function evaluations can improve step-size selection along a fixed direction. Importantly, these improvements occur with the same search scale, since all methods use β=1.\beta=1. Thus, the ZFO methods are not benefiting from a larger trust region; rather, they are using local curvature behavior to select more effective intermediate steps within the same update interval. This is most visible in the separation between Taylor2, Taylor3, and Padé3 relative to FO, showing that the additional curvature information can meaningfully alter the chosen step even when the learning rate is fixed. The behavior of Padé2 further supports this interpretation; among the ZFO methods, Padé2 is the most restricted in the sense it contains only a linear numerator and denominator. Consequently, when β=1\beta=1, Padé2 often selects a step close to the standard FO update, making it the ZFO variant most similar to FO. This trend is reflected in the final performance summaries with Taylor3 performing the best in both environments – Taylor2 and Padé3 trailing close behind. Overall, these toy results provide validation of the ZFO step-selection mechanism before moving to higher-dimensional models.

Learning Rate Sensitivity Curves. Figure 8 establishes that ZFO’s gains rise from intelligent step selection rather than a hidden learning-rate effect. In each panel, we plot ZFO trajectories alongside FO FT runs surrounding the base learning rate to compare against ZFO runs. The three panels highlight complementary behaviors; e.g., Qwen on OpenBookQA shows ZFO trajectories outperforming FO runs with the same nominal search regions, reinforcing the extremely large margin in Table 1. Phi-2 on Svamp shows ZFO trajectories steadily improving over the FO baselines. Llama on AsDiv shows that the most conservative FO baseline eventually destabilizes during training, whereas ZFO methods remain stable. Together, these curves indicate that ZFO occupies a regime that FO cannot reach by fixed learning rates.

Bound vs. Learning Rate Ablation. Figure 9 reports the full ablation over the learning rate α\alpha and search bound β\beta that was summarized in the main paper. We sweep both hyperparameters across all four ZFO methods on Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B, evaluating after 10 epochs on subsets (512/256 train/eval) of GSM8K and SVAMP. As discussed in the main paper, at smaller learning rates, increasing β\beta produces near-monotonic improvements, while at larger learning rates the gains saturate as the search region RR grows too large. Comparing (α=10−6,β=5)(\alpha=10^{-6},\beta=5) against (α=5×10−6,β=1)(\alpha=5\times 10^{-6},\beta=1) also shows that configurations with the same nominal search region yield different final performance, indicating that α\alpha and β\beta are complementary rather than interchangeable. See §C.1.1 for the formal implementation of R.R.

Examining Figure 9 closely, we observe the high-reward region forms a diagonal band that shifts toward smaller β\beta as α\alpha grows. At α=10−6\alpha=10^{-6} and α=5×10−6\alpha=5\times 10^{-6}, performance improves steadily as β\beta increases from 11 to 100100 across all four methods. At α=10−5\alpha=10^{-5}, the best results pull back toward small β.\beta. Combining the largest bound with α=10−5\alpha=10^{-5} collapses the reward to near-zero for almost all methods.

Cross-Setting Improvement Frequency. As an additional appendix diagnostic, we summarize how often each ZFO variant improves over the corresponding FO baseline across the reported evaluation settings in Table 9. Across the 12 main result settings and the 4 Qwen sub-study settings, Taylor2, Taylor3, Padé2, and Padé3 improve over FO in 14/16, 7/16, 13/16, and 14/16 settings, respectively. This supports the view that ZFO is driven by a recurring advantage in adaptive step selection across settings.

Additional first-order baselines.

To compare ZFO with different learning-rate adaptation strategies, we additionally evaluate AdamW with a warmup-cosine schedule [30] and the parameter-free Prodigy optimizer [37] in Table 10. We preserve the Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B model, dataset-specific training configurations, GRPO objective, evaluation protocol, and seeds used in the corresponding main and sub-study experiments. For AdamW with cosine decay, the learning rate selected for the constant-rate FO baseline is used as the peak rate; it gets reached by linear warmup over the first 10%10\% of optimizer steps and then decayed to zero according to a cosine schedule. Prodigy instead uses its recommended configuration with adjustment factor 1.01.0, dcoef=1.0d_{\mathrm{coef}}=1.0, decoupled weight decay 0.010.01, and no external learning-rate schedule. To contextualize these baselines within the range of behavior exhibited by ZFO, the table also reports the lowest- and highest-mean ZFO variants for each dataset.

Table 10 shows that the strongest ZFO variant outperforms both AdamW with cosine decay and Prodigy across all eight datasets on Qwen. AdamW with cosine decay remains the stronger of the two additional FO baselines, while Prodigy consistently trails both the scheduled AdamW baseline and the best ZFO method. However, the worst-performing ZFO variant falls below AdamW with cosine decay on several datasets, indicating that the advantage does not arise uniformly across every local model. Overall, these results suggest that ZFO can improve over many step-adaptive baselines, while also signaling that the choice of local approximation remains important.

ZFO Sequential Line Search. The four ZFO methods in the main paper select a step using a local model constructed from a fixed budget of two probes. ZFO-Seq extends this design to a sequential budget of k>2k>2 fixed-batch evaluations. The first two probes construct the initial model M∈{T2,T3,P2,P3}M\in\{T_{2},T_{3},P_{2},P_{3}\} as in Algorithm 1, and the remaining k−2k-2 probes are spent refining the model’s proposal.

At each refinement step, the current candidate maximizer is evaluated on the shared minibatch StS_{t}, and a new candidate is proposed by fitting a parabola through the best evaluated point in ItI_{t} and its two nearest evaluated neighbors, aligning with safeguarded successive parabolic interpolation [8]. The returned step is the best evaluated point rather than a model maximizer. Every candidate must survive an actual evaluation of ϕt\phi_{t} before it can be selected. Since (0,ϕt​(0))∈Et(0,\phi_{t}(0))\in E_{t} by construction, ZFO-Seq guarantees ϕt​(st)≥ϕt​(0)\phi_{t}(s_{t})\geq\phi_{t}(0) at every iteration, a monotone non-decrease of the empirical surrogate. This replaces the model-selection gap ϕ⁡(sϕ)−ϕ⁡(sM)\phi(s_{\phi})-\phi(s_{M}) with the gap attained by the best of kk evaluated points, which shrinks under refinement. Algorithm 2 summarizes the procedure.

Table 11 reports the evaluation accuracy for a variety of line-search methods on the Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B model (seed 100, configuration C, learning rate 1e-5, search bound β=3\beta=3). Each ZFO-Seq model used P3P_{3} as its default initialization.

Table 11 compares ZFO-Seq against several established line-search methods. ZFO-Seq achieves the strongest result on CODAH, while remaining within approximately two points of the best-performing method on both ARC-Challenge and SVAMP. Armijo and Barzilai-Borwein remain slightly stronger on these latter settings, whereas Polyak and PLS generally trail ZFO-Seq. Thus, ZFO-Seq is competitive with classical line-search and adaptive step-size methods across the three evaluated settings.

Unit-Bound Ablation. To determine whether ZFO benefits require a search interval larger than the standard first-order update, we additionally evaluate the four ZFO models with the bound fixed to β=1\beta=1 on Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B. Under this setting, ZFO may shorten or reshape the AdamW update but cannot select a step beyond the endpoint corresponding to the nominal FO displacement. ARC-Challenge and StrategyQA use three-epoch versions of configuration a, while ASDiv uses a three-epoch version of configuration c; we denote these shortened configurations by a’ and c’, respectively. Their batch size, group size, context length, and maximum output length otherwise remain unchanged. All methods use the fixed RLVR settings in Table 4, including perturbation scale ϵ=10−3\epsilon=10^{-3}, and results are averaged over seeds {100,101,102}\{100,101,102\}. Table 12 reports the resulting final evaluation accuracy.

Table 12 shows that ZFO can modify training behavior even when it is not permitted to move beyond the nominal FO update. On ARC-Challenge, all four ZFO variants outperform AdamW at the shared learning rate of 10−510^{-5}; however, reducing the separately tuned FO learning rate to 5×10−65\times 10^{-6} raises its accuracy to 55.1255.12, so the ARC result is best interpreted as ZFO recovering a competitive step scale. On StrategyQA, Taylor3 performs best at 74.8774.87, followed by Taylor2 and Padé2, whereas Padé3 falls below FO. On ASDiv, FO remains narrowly best, although Taylor2, Padé2, and Padé3 remain within 0.260.26 points. Thus, β=1\beta=1 is sufficient for gains in some settings, but we argue that the ZFO methods’ largest gains arise from the ability to safely navigate larger learning rates.

Location of ZFO Steps. We next examine where the ZFO methods select steps within the search interval It=[0,R]I_{t}=[0,R]. This diagnostic distinguishes between selecting no update (st=0s_{t}=0), the largest permitted update (st=Rs_{t}=R), and an interior step. Because numerical solutions may lie arbitrarily close to an endpoint, we report both the exact interior frequency, 0<st<R0<s_{t}<R, and a 1%-trimmed interior frequency, 0.01<st/R<0.990.01<s_{t}/R<0.99. We also report the median normalized step st/Rs_{t}/R. Statistics are computed within each run. Table 13 summarizes the β=1\beta=1 Family-B cohort, consisting of 48 runs across four configurations, and the fixed-β=3\beta=3 cohort, consisting of 108 runs across nine model-dataset pairs.

Table 13 reveals distinct step-selection behaviors across the four ZFO models. Taylor3 makes the most frequent use of the interval interior under both bounds. Its exact interior frequency increases from 65.83%65.83\% at β=1\beta=1 to 80.77%80.77\% at β=3\beta=3, while its 1%-trimmed interior frequency rises more substantially from 23.88%23.88\% to 70.28%70.28\%. The difference between the two interior measures at β=1\beta=1, together with a median normalized step of 0.001560.00156, indicates that many of its nominally interior selections lie close to the zero endpoint. At β=3\beta=3, however, most selections remain interior even after trimming, showing that Taylor3 frequently chooses steps that are meaningfully separated from both boundaries.

The other models rely more heavily on endpoint selections. Taylor2 most often selects the full step st=Rs_{t}=R, doing so in 57.66%57.66\% of updates at β=1\beta=1 and 64.59%64.59\% at β=3\beta=3. Padé2 never selects an interior point in either cohort and therefore acts empirically as a binary rule between st=0s_{t}=0 and st=Rs_{t}=R. Padé3 also remains largely endpoint-driven. The median of textttPadé3 shifts from zero at β=1\beta=1 to the upper endpoint at β=3\beta=3. Its fallback frequency simultaneously increases from 12.49%12.49\% to 54.95%54.95\%, indicating that the quadratic safeguard becomes substantially more important over the larger search interval. Overall, the results show that the cubic Taylor model uses higher-order information primarily to select intermediate step lengths, whereas the remaining models more often use their local approximations to choose between suppressing and taking the full permitted update.
